newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel vows to build settlement despite warnings.
newsitem.headline: Israel vows to build settlement despite warnings.

text.p: Israel vowed on Sunday to break ground on a Jewish settlement despite a conciliatory visit by the king of Jordan and warnings the project threatened to spark Palestinian violence and freeze Middle East peace moves.

Jordan's King Hussein flew to Israel to console families of seven schoolgirls slaughtered by one of his soldiers at the border last week and to defuse tensions with Israel's leader Benjamin Netanyahu.
The king, like some Palestinian officials, warned last week of bloodshed if Israel went ahead with unilateral plans to begin building a Jewish settlement on the outskirts of Arab East Jerusalem.
Just before the king went into a meeting with Netanyahu, Israel's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh insisted Israel's government would not yield to "threats" and "pressures" over the settlement issue.

Israel's Deputy Housing Minister Meir Porush said he hoped work on the 6,500 houses for Jews would begin on Monday at the hilltop site on the outskirts of Arab East Jerusalem known as Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic -- Har Homa to Israelis.
"I cannot tell you the exact date when the work will begin. The work is supposed to begin this week," Naveh told Israel Television. "I expect it will be this week."

Netanyahu says the settlement reasserts an Israeli right to all of Jerusalem and insists Israeli-PLO peace deals do not bar the construction. Palestinians claim East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967, as the capital of a future state.

Israel's police chief Assaf Hefetz added his own warning on Sunday, saying police shared the fears and assessments of other Israeli security forces about the prospect of violence if the building project went ahead.
"Construction there could heat up the situation and lead to a deterioration in relations," Hefetz said on Israel Radio.

Netanyahu sparked an outburst of violence last September when he punched open a new entrance to a tunnel near Islamic shrines in East Jerusalem. The bloodshed claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.

As it happens Monday -- the scheduled day of groundbreaking -- is also the day that Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had agreed to launch negotiations on the future of Jerusalem and other tough "final-status" issues.
Negotiators on both sides acknowledged no time and place had been set for starting those talks.

"Israel's bulldozing of Jabal Abu Ghneim land tomorrow is a unilateral attempt to end the agreement and a war of bulldozers against the peace process," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters.
Israel's Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi raised tensions further on Saturday, warning Arafat he faced possible expulsion from Gaza, where he has ruled since 1994, should he launch a wave of unrest.

"Whoever launches violence could very quickly find himself packing a suitcase and travelling back and forth on the line from Tunis to Baghdad like he (Arafat) did for many years," Hanegbi told supporters in remarks on Saturday.

Hanegbi's counterpart in Arafat's Palestinian Authority, Freih Abu Medeen, cancelled a meeting with the Israeli minister over the remarks. Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said he regretted Hanegbi's remarks.

European Middle East envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos said after meeting Arafat on Sunday he hoped to persuade Israel and the Palestinians to accept a confidence-building proposal to solve the crisis. He did not elaborate on the measure.
